items.title: An ambulance's pitch drops as it passes you — and that drop is the Doppler effect
items.claim: An approaching ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched than its 'true' frequency; once it passes, the pitch suddenly drops. The shift is the Doppler effect, and it provides a quantitative way to measure radial velocity.

options.text: The siren plays different notes as it moves

Sound waves emitted by a source moving toward you are compressed (higher frequency, higher pitch); waves from a source moving away are stretched (lower frequency, lower pitch). The shift Δf/f equals v/c_sound
Your ears change sensitivity with movement
The siren only changes pitch in air

items.reveal:
For a source moving with speed v toward a stationary observer, the observed frequency is f_observed = f_source × c / (c - v), where c is the speed of sound. For source moving away, replace minus by plus.

At 30 m/s (a fast vehicle) and 343 m/s (speed of sound), the shift is about ±9 percent — easily heard as a pitch change of around a semitone.

The same effect applies to light. Astronomers measure stellar and galactic radial velocities by Doppler shifts of spectral lines. Most galaxies show redshifted spectra: they are moving away. This is how Hubble (1929) showed the universe is expanding.

Doppler weather radar bounces microwaves off raindrops and measures the frequency shift to find wind speeds at altitude. Police radar guns use the same principle to measure car speeds.
items.why: The Doppler effect is taught as 'pitch changes'. It is a universal feature of any wave and underlies tools from speed cameras to cosmology.

items.title: Every measurement in a working lab traces back to seven international standards
items.claim: Every length, mass, temperature, current, time, light intensity and amount of substance measurement at any modern lab can be traced through calibration chains back to seven defined units maintained by international bodies. Calibration is what makes measurements comparable across labs.
items.prompt: What does 'traceable' mean for a measurement?

options.text: The instrument was calibrated against a reference standard, which itself was calibrated against a higher-tier standard, all the way back to the SI definition. Every step has a documented uncertainty
The instrument has a serial number
The measurement was published in a journal

items.reveal_title: Traceability chains and the redefined SI
items.reveal:
In 2019 the SI was redefined so all seven base units are now derived from fundamental constants: the speed of light defines the metre, the Planck constant defines the kilogram (since 2019, replacing the platinum-iridium reference cylinder), the Boltzmann constant defines the kelvin, and so on.

A national metrology institute (NPL in the UK, NIST in the US) maintains primary realisations of these units. Industry calibration labs are calibrated against these primaries. Working labs send instruments to industry labs for periodic calibration.

When you read a balance display in a school lab, the number you see has a chain of calibration certificates behind it linking it back to the Planck constant via a Kibble balance.
items.why: Calibration is treated as paperwork. It is the substrate that makes any quantitative claim comparable across labs, countries and decades.

items.title: An electron interferes with itself
items.claim: Fire electrons one at a time at a screen with two slits. With BOTH slits open, the pattern that builds up is the classic interference fringe — even though only one electron is in flight at any moment.
items.prompt: What gets in the way of saying 'each electron goes through one slit or the other'?

options.text: Nothing — each electron does go through one slit

If you measure which slit each electron uses, the interference pattern disappears — the electron behaves as a particle. Without the measurement, the wavefunction passes through both slits and self-interferes
Multiple electrons collide in flight and create the pattern
The fringe pattern is an artefact of the screen, not the electrons

items.reveal:
Before measurement, the electron's wavefunction is a superposition of 'through slit 1' and 'through slit 2' paths. The interference fringes are the result of these amplitudes adding and cancelling at the detector.

Add any apparatus capable of detecting which slit the electron went through — even in principle — and the interference vanishes. The state has become entangled with the detector and no longer interferes with itself.

This is the heart of quantum mechanics. It's not about ignorance. It's not 'we don't know which slit'. It's that, until measured, the electron is in BOTH paths in a coherent superposition that has measurable effects (the fringes).
items.why: Particles have definite positions in classical physics. Quantum particles don't — their position is a probability distribution that depends on what you can in principle know.
